p: The Spirit is sent into 'our' hearts in the older text and 'your' hearts in the Byzantine text.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.plain: into our hearts

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV); Burton calls 'your' a Western and Syrian reading
readings.plain: into your hearts

why: The Plain English Translation follows 'our'. It is the reading the critical editions print, and Burton (1921) judges 'our' 'undoubtedly to be preferred' to 'your'. It is also the harder reading: after 'you are sons' a scribe would smooth the sentence to 'your hearts', while 'our' changes person in mid-sentence. Paul may be including himself and other Jewish believers beside the Gentile 'you' (see the note on 4:6).

a: you are also an heir, through God
t: Heir 'through God' or 'of God through Christ'?
p: Older manuscripts say 'an heir through God'; later ones say 'an heir of God through Christ'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the NET Bible's note lists Papyrus 46, Sinaiticus (first hand), A, Vaticanus, C (first hand), 33, 1739, the Latin and Bohairic versions and Clement for 'through God'
readings.plain: you are also an heir, through God

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'heir of God through Christ'); the NET Bible's note lists a later hand of Sinaiticus, a later hand of C, D, the Byzantine majority, an Old Latin copy and the Syriac for 'of God through Christ'
readings.en: an heir of God through Christ
readings.plain: you are also an heir of God through Christ

why: The Plain English Translation follows the shorter reading. The NET Bible's note says 'through God' is unusual and 'certainly prompted scribes to alter it', and that its witnesses are among the most important in the New Testament. A scribe would find it easy to fix by writing the familiar 'heir of God through Christ' (Romans 8:17). The longer reading is an easy and natural correction.
b: The sense is nearly the same either way: God is the one who makes the believer an heir. The KJV reader will find 'heir of God through Christ', which echoes Romans 8:17.

a: The test that my body brought you
p: Did Paul's weakness test the Galatians, or was it his own test? One pronoun changes.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.orig: τὸν πειρασμὸν ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου
readings.plain: The test that my body brought you

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: τὸν πειρασμόν μου τὸν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου
readings.en: my test, the one in my flesh
readings.plain: My test, which was in my body,

why: The Plain English Translation follows 'your test in my flesh', the reading the critical editions print, and the harder one. It means: my body was a test for you, a thing you might have rejected. 'My test' is the easier phrase, and a scribe could have changed 'your' to 'my' because it seems more natural for Paul to speak of his own trial.
b: The Plain English Translation's 'brought you' tries to keep the unusual 'your test'. The KJV follows the other reading ('my temptation which was in my flesh').

a: So where is that joy of yours now?
p: Two readings of the opening words of 4:15 change a present question into a past one.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; Burton lists Sinaiticus, A, B, C, F, G, P, 33, the Vulgate and Old Latin f g, the Bohairic and Armenian versions, and Jerome
readings.plain: So where is that joy of yours now?

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (the Byzantine also adds 'would' later in the verse); Burton lists D, K, L, most later manuscripts, the Gothic version, Chrysostom, Augustine and others
readings.orig: τίς οὖν ἦν ὁ μακαρισμὸς ὑμῶν;
readings.plain: So what was that joy of yours?

why: The Plain English Translation follows 'Where, then, is', the reading the critical editions print. Both readings are old, but the difference is small in meaning: Paul is asking what has become of the Galatians' early gladness. Burton thinks 'tis' arose by a copyist's slip ('POU' turned into 'TIS') and finds the evidence for 'pou' much the stronger.

p: A small change of a word: 'children' or the more tender 'little children'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tregelles
readings.plain: My children

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'My little children')
readings.plain: My little children

why: The Plain English Translation follows tekna, 'children', which the SBL and NA28 print. The editors who print teknia (the Tyndale House GNT among them) take it as Paul's tender form, used elsewhere (1 John 2:1). The decision is close. Either way, Paul speaks as a parent in labor.

a: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia.
p: Three forms of the sentence: 'Hagar is Sinai', 'For Hagar is Sinai', and 'For Sinai is in Arabia', with no Hagar.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort; Lightfoot (1865) lists A, B, D, E and a few cursives for this form
readings.orig: τὸ δὲ Ἁγὰρ Σινᾶ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ
readings.en: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia
readings.plain: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia.

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia'); Lightfoot lists K, L, P, most cursives, both Syriac versions and Chrysostom, Theodore, Theodoret and Theophylact
readings.orig: τὸ γὰρ Ἅγαρ Σινᾶ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ
readings.en: For Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia
readings.plain: For Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia.

readings.w: Lightfoot (1865) lists Sinaiticus, C, F, G, the cursive 17, the Old Latin copies f and g, the Vulgate ('Sina enim mons est in Arabia'), the Ethiopic and Armenian versions, Origen, Epiphanius, Cyril, John of Damascus, and Latin writers including Augustine and Jerome
readings.orig: τὸ γὰρ Σινᾶ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ
readings.en: For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia
readings.plain: For Mount Sinai is in Arabia.

why: The Plain English Translation follows the text with 'Hagar', the form the major critical editions print (they differ only between 'Now' and 'For'). The omission is not weakly supported: Lightfoot called it the reading with 'the strongest, because the most varied, testimony', argued that a scribe had added 'Hagar' from the context, and noted that Bentley and Lachmann also preferred the omission, while Westcott and Hort kept it only in their margin. The Plain English Translation keeps 'Hagar' with the editions, so this is a close call. Lightfoot's lists are from 1865 and do not include the papyri.
b: If 'Hagar' is not in the original, Paul would be saying only that Sinai is in Arabia, and the link between Hagar and the mountain would come from the context. The Vulgate itself reads this way. The question matters for the sense: it decides whether Paul himself calls Hagar 'Sinai' or leaves the link to the reader.

t: 'Our mother' or 'the mother of us all'?
p: The KJV's 'the mother of us all' is in the Byzantine text, not in the older manuscripts.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.plain: She is our mother.

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'the mother of us all')
readings.en: who is the mother of all of us
readings.plain: She is the mother of us all.

why: The Plain English Translation follows the shorter text that the critical editions print. The longer reading 'of all of us' is the Byzantine reading, and may be a natural expansion; that is an inference from how the editions split, not something a witness list shows.

a: As for you, brothers, you are children born through the promise, as Isaac was.
p: The older text says 'you are children of promise'; the Byzantine text says 'we are'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles; the NET Bible's note lists Papyrus 46, Vaticanus, the first hand of D, F, G, 33, 1739 and the Sahidic version for 'you'
readings.plain: As for you, brothers, you are children born through the promise, as Isaac was.

readings.w: Westcott-Hort, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'Now we, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of promise'); the NET Bible's note lists Sinaiticus, A, C, a later hand of D, the Byzantine majority, the Latin, Syriac and Bohairic for 'we'
readings.plain: As for us, brothers, we are children born through the promise, as Isaac was.

why: The Plain English Translation follows 'you'. The letter has been speaking to the Galatians as 'you' (4:19-21), and the verse that follows addresses them again (4:31 says 'we'). Scribes may have changed 'you' to 'we' to match 4:26 and 4:31. The difference is small. The NET Bible's note says most manuscripts read 'we'.

a: Christ has set us free, to live in freedom. So hold your ground, and do not get tangled up again in a yoke of slavery.
t: A different order and joining of the words
p: The older text is a short statement and a command; the Byzantine text joins them in one long sentence.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.orig: τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ ἡμᾶς Χριστὸς ἠλευθέρωσεν· στήκετε οὖν
readings.en: For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm, then
readings.plain: Christ has set us free, to live in freedom. So hold your ground, and do not get tangled up again in a yoke of slavery.

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free')
readings.orig: τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ οὖν ᾗ Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἠλευθέρωσεν, στήκετε
readings.en: Stand firm, then, in the freedom with which Christ has set us free
readings.plain: So hold your ground in the freedom that Christ has given us, and do not get tangled up again in a yoke of slavery.

why: The Plain English Translation follows the older text, in which the first clause stands alone: 'for freedom Christ freed us'. The Byzantine form is smoother, with the relative clause 'in which' and the 'then' placed first. The smoother reading is probably a scribe's tidying. The wording also fits the verses around it: 4:31 says 'we are free', and 5:1 states the purpose.
b: Some witnesses also move the 'therefore' or the word for 'free' in other ways, and the break between chapters 4 and 5 sits at different places in the manuscripts. The meaning of the verse does not change.

p: The KJV list begins 'Adultery, fornication'. The older text begins with 'sexual immorality'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.plain: They are sexual immorality

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness')
readings.en: adultery, sexual immorality, uncleanness, shameless living
readings.plain: They are adultery, sexual immorality

why: The Plain English Translation follows the shorter list. 'Adultery' was easy to add: it is the first of the three sins in lists like Matthew 15:19 and 1 Corinthians 6:9, and a scribe might add it to fill out a familiar pattern. The critical editions leave it out. Adultery is in any case included in 'sexual immorality' (porneia), a broad word.

p: The KJV list says 'envyings, murders, drunkenness'. The SBL and NA28 leave out 'murders'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort; the NET Bible's note lists Papyrus 46, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, 33, 81, 323, 945 and the Sahidic version for the shorter text
readings.plain: envy, drunkenness

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'envyings, murders, drunkenness'); the NET Bible's note lists A, C, D, F, G, Psi, 1739, 1881, the Byzantine majority and the Latin for the longer text
readings.plain: envy, murders, drunkenness

why: The Plain English Translation follows the SBL and NA28, the shorter reading. The case for 'murders' is real, though: the Greek words phthonoi ('envy') and phonoi ('murders') look and sound almost the same, so a scribe's eye could skip one by accident. The NET Bible's note says the omitting witnesses are of 'the highest degree' but that this kind of skip may well explain the shorter reading, and the Tyndale House GNT prints the longer one. The sense of the list does not depend on it, since murder is condemned elsewhere (Romans 1:29).
b: The pair is a play on sound in Greek (phthonoi, phonoi), which suggests that Paul may have written both.

p: Some editions read 'those of Christ Jesus', others 'those of Christ'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus; the NET Bible's note lists Papyrus 46, D, F, G, the Latin and Syriac versions and the Byzantine text for 'Christ' without 'Jesus'
readings.plain: Those who are Christ's

readings.w: NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the NET Bible's note lists Sinaiticus, A, B, C, P, Psi, 33, 1739 and the Coptic versions for 'Christ Jesus'
readings.plain: Those who are Christ Jesus's

why: The Plain English Translation follows the shorter form. The editions are split: the SBLGNT, the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus have the shorter form, and the NA28, NA27, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles have the longer. The NET Bible's note prefers the shorter form too. The meaning does not change.

a: If you do, you will fulfill
p: A one-letter difference makes the verb a promise or a command.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles
readings.plain: If you do, you will fulfill

readings.w: Westcott-Hort, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'and so fulfil the law of Christ')
readings.plain: In this way, fulfill

why: The Plain English Translation follows the future 'you will fulfill'. The two readings differ by one vowel, the future indicative anaplerosete against the aorist imperative anaplerosate. Both make sense: the future states the result of carrying each other's loads, the imperative restates the command. The editions split as shown, and the Byzantine text has the imperative. One possible reason for the imperative is that a scribe was drawn to the many commands around it (6:1-6), which would make the future the less obvious reading; that is an inference.

p: One letter turns 'as we have opportunity' into 'while we may have opportunity'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
readings.plain: whenever we have the chance

readings.w: Westcott-Hort
readings.plain: whenever we may have the chance

why: The Plain English Translation follows the reading of nearly every edition. The difference is between an indicative and a subjunctive after hos, and the sense is almost the same: Paul urges them to do good while there is time.

a: The very ones who are having themselves circumcised
p: The tense of one word changes who Paul is describing: Gentiles taking circumcision now, or people already circumcised.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Textus Receptus; Burton (1921) lists Sinaiticus, A, C, D, the Old Latin f, the Vulgate, the Syriac, Sahidic and Armenian versions, Marcion, Chrysostom and Theodoret for the present
readings.plain: The very ones who are having themselves circumcised

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text; Burton lists Vaticanus, L, the Old Latin d and g, the Gothic and Bohairic versions, Victorinus, Augustine and Jerome for the perfect (F and G, he says, have impossible forms that probably witness to the perfect)
readings.plain: The very ones who have been circumcised

why: The Plain English Translation follows the present participle, which the SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles print. The perfect participle is printed by the Tyndale House GNT and is the Byzantine reading. Burton's lists (above) show the witnesses divided, and he calls the external evidence 'not decisive'; he judges that a copyist would find the perfect an unobjectionable reading, so the present is the likelier original. The two readings point to different people. Present: people who are now being circumcised, or who take circumcision on, such as Gentile converts. Perfect: people who have already been circumcised, that is, Jews or earlier converts. The choice affects who the agitators were, but the sentence says the same thing about both groups: they do not keep the law. The note on this verse gives the debate. This is a close call.
b: This is one of the most discussed variants for deciding who the agitators were. If 'those having been circumcised', the agitators are Jews or Jewish converts. If 'those being circumcised', they may include Gentiles who have accepted circumcision (Munck).

a: Circumcision is nothing, and so is uncircumcision.
t: A short form and a longer one
p: The Byzantine text copies the wording of 5:6 here.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; the NET Bible's note lists Papyrus 46, Vaticanus, Psi, 33, 1175, 1505, 1739 (first hand) and several church fathers for the shorter form
readings.orig: οὔτε γὰρ περιτομή τί ἐστιν οὔτε ἀκροβυστία
readings.en: For neither circumcision is anything nor uncircumcision
readings.plain: Circumcision is nothing, and so is uncircumcision.

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision'); the NET Bible's note lists Sinaiticus, A, C, D, F, G, 1881, the Byzantine majority, the Latin and Bohairic for 'in Christ Jesus'
readings.orig: ἐν γὰρ Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ οὔτε περιτομή τι ἰσχύει, οὔτε ἀκροβυστία
readings.en: For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any strength nor uncircumcision
readings.plain: In Christ Jesus, circumcision has no strength, and neither does uncircumcision.

why: The Plain English Translation follows the shorter form. The Byzantine wording is almost exactly 5:6 ('In Christ Jesus, circumcision has no strength and neither does uncircumcision'), and the NET Bible's note judges that the longer reading is probably a harmonization to 5:6. The shorter, different form is also the one that fits the next clause, 'a new creation'.

p: A short title in the older text is longer in the Byzantine text.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.plain: carrying the marks of Jesus

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'the marks of the Lord Jesus')
readings.en: the marks of the Lord Jesus
readings.plain: carrying the marks of the Lord Jesus

why: The Plain English Translation follows the shorter title, which the critical editions print. Scribes liked fuller titles. Paul's plain 'Jesus' is what we might expect from him in speaking of the man who was crucified.

a: Brothers, may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.
p: The KJV letter ends with a line saying it was written from Rome. That line is a later addition.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text
readings.orig: μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν, ἀδελφοί· ἀμήν.
readings.plain: Brothers, may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

readings.w: Textus Receptus and some late manuscripts add a closing line (KJV: 'Unto the Galatians written from Rome')
readings.en: To the Galatians, written from Rome
readings.plain: Brothers, may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen. To the Galatians. Written from Rome.

why: The Plain English Translation stops at 'Amen'. The closing lines in some manuscripts are not Paul's. They are notes added by later copyists, and they differ from manuscript to manuscript. Rome is almost certainly wrong: Paul's own place of writing is not given in the letter, and the suggestions vary from Ephesus to Corinth to Antioch.
b: Such 'subscriptions' appear after most of Paul's letters in later manuscripts and are of little value as history. See also the introduction to the letter for the date and place of writing.
